# Wrangler: pico data store

# Pico data store

*Ruleset: `io.picolabs.pds`, installed on every pico. For every event and function, see the [API reference](/rulesets/io.picolabs.pds).*

[Relationships](/wrangler/relationships) answer "how do two picos talk to each other?" The pico data store (PDS) answers "where does a pico keep its data, and how do rulesets read and write it consistently?"

Without PDS, each application ruleset makes its own entity variables (`ent:contactInfo`, `ent:thingInfo`, …). Display names end up in Wrangler, contact cards in one ruleset, configuration in another. PDS is one shared data service on every pico, with three layers:

| Layer | Entity variable | Purpose |
|-------|-----------------|---------|
| Profile | `ent:profile` | This pico's display identity: name, description, photo. A person's profile only if this pico stands for a person |
| General | `ent:general` | Namespaced key-value data for apps and domains |
| Settings | `ent:settings` | Per-ruleset configuration, keyed by rid |

Design principles:

- **PDS owns the data.** Apps don't write `ent:profile`, `ent:general`, or `ent:settings` themselves. They raise `pds` events; PDS rules store the data and announce the change.
- **Reads go through shared functions.** Other rulesets `use module io.picolabs.pds` and call its functions (`profile`, `items`, `config_value`, …).
- **Writes are events.** Raise `pds:updated_profile`, `pds:new_data_available`, and so on; select `pds:profile_updated`, `pds:data_added`, and so on to react.
- **One PDS per pico.** The engine installs it on the root pico, and Wrangler installs it on every child.

PDS doesn't replace relationships, channels, or Wrangler; it complements them. Relationships are the wire; PDS is the notebook each pico keeps about itself. Not everything belongs in it: see the next section.

## What belongs in PDS (and what doesn't)

PDS is a pico's shared data plane, but application rulesets still have their own entity variables. Use PDS when the data is shared, queried, or part of the pico's display identity. Keep data in the app's ruleset when it is private, derived, short-lived, or changes very often.

### Profile, on every pico

Put in the profile (`pds:updated_profile`, read with `pds:profile()`):

| Data | Examples |
|------|----------|
| Display name | Labels for things, communities, owners, and registries in UI lists and notifications |
| Short description | A community's blurb, a thing's subtitle |
| Photo or avatar | An owner's photo, a thing's icon |
| Contact details (on an owner's pico) | Email and phone, for notifications |

The profile is the stable surface other picos read: frameworks, notifications, and peers use `wrangler:picoQuery(eci, "io.picolabs.pds", "profile", …)` without knowing each app's layout. When PDS is installed, it copies the Wrangler name into the profile if the profile has none.

In application rulesets, prefer `pds:profile("name")` to `wrangler:name()` for anything shown to people.

### General data

Put in general (`pds:new_data_available`, by namespace and key):

| Situation | Example |
|-----------|---------|
| Two or more rulesets on the same pico need the data | A contact card read by a lost-and-found app and by a public query channel |
| Other picos read it with `picoQuery(..., "io.picolabs.pds", "items", …)` | A registry's ECI stored on a thing, for tag lookup |
| A namespace documented for others to rely on | `general.safeandmine.contact`, `general.sensor.last_reading` |

Keep in the app's own entity variables (and raise the app's own events):

| Situation | Example |
|-----------|---------|
| One ruleset writes it and nothing else reads it | An internal list of channels, pending UI state |
| A cache rebuilt from relationships and PDS reads | `ent:thingInfo` on a thing pico |
| An index rebuilt from Wrangler events | A hub's list of the things and communities it holds (the canonical name is in each child's profile) |
| Short-lived UI state | Layout, colors, badge counts, notification inbox rows |
| High-volume telemetry | Raw sensor readings. Use PDS general only if other rulesets must query the latest value |

### Settings

Put in settings (`pds:add_settings`, keyed by ruleset rid):

- Per-app configuration and feature flags (`shareEmail`, thresholds, notification switches).
- Data the owning ruleset reads with `pds:config_value("key")`, which uses the calling ruleset's rid.

Keep operational state (the last run's id, timers, in-flight maps) in the app's ruleset, unless another ruleset must read it.

### A checklist

- Needs a stable API that other rulesets or picos read? PDS: profile, general, or settings, by shape.
- The pico's display identity in UIs or notifications? The profile.
- Only this ruleset touches it? The app's own entity variables.
- Rebuilt from relationship, Wrangler, or framework events? A derived cache in the app's ruleset, not duplicated in PDS.
- Layout, cache, or scratch state? The app's own entity variables.

### Mirroring (planned)

Mirrors of a pico (copies kept elsewhere) are planned around a selective event log: replaying Wrangler, framework, and `pds` events, plus events apps opt in, rebuilds a pico's state. `pds` writes are good events for that log. A PDS snapshot (profile, general, settings, and installed rulesets) is a simpler export. App entity variables are views rebuilt on replay. Don't move data into PDS only for mirroring; move it when it is shared.

## Using PDS in KRL

In a ruleset that reads PDS data on the same pico:

```krl
meta {
  use module io.picolabs.pds alias pds
}
```

To read PDS on another pico, query it with `wrangler:picoQuery` on a channel whose query policy allows `io.picolabs.pds`:

```krl
displayName = wrangler:picoQuery(thing_eci, "io.picolabs.pds", "profile", {"key": "name"}){"profile"}
```

When PDS is installed, it creates a channel tagged `pds` that allows `pds` events and `io.picolabs.pds` queries, for HTTP access. On the root pico, it also makes sure the channel exists each time the engine starts. The developer UI's channel doesn't allow PDS queries.

## Reading data

The functions return a map with `status` (`"success"` or `"failed"`) and the data under `profile`, `general`, or `settings`.

### Profile

`profile(key)` reads this pico's profile: how the pico presents itself. Each pico has its own. A thing's name isn't its owner's name unless an app copies it there.

| Call | Returns |
|------|---------|
| `profile()` | The whole profile |
| `profile("name")` | One field, under `profile` |

```krl
allProfile = pds:profile(){"profile"}
name = pds:profile("name"){"profile"}
```

An empty profile looks like this; the default `photo` is a placeholder image, as a `data:` URI:

```json
{"name": "", "description": "", "photo": "data:image/svg+xml;base64,..."}
```

### General items

`items(namespace, key)`:

| Call | Returns |
|------|---------|
| `items(null, null)` | All of `ent:general` (use sparingly) |
| `items("myapp", null)` | Every key in the `myapp` namespace |
| `items("myapp", "contact")` | One value |

```krl
card = pds:items("safeandmine", "contact"){"general"}
allTags = pds:items("safeandmine", null){"general"}
```

### Settings

| Function | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `settings(rid, key, detail)` | A ruleset's settings entry, or part of it |
| `setting_data(rid)` | The `Data` map for a ruleset |
| `setting_data_value(rid, setKey)` | One key in it |
| `config_value(setKey)` | One key of the calling ruleset's own data |

`config_value` lets a ruleset read its own preferences without naming its rid:

```krl
threshold = pds:config_value("threshold")
```

## Writing data

### The profile

Raise `pds:updated_profile` with any of the profile's fields. It merges into the profile; fields you leave out keep their values. PDS sets `_created` on the first write and `_modified` on every one.

```krl
raise pds event "updated_profile" attributes {
  "name": "Blue Backpack",
  "description": "Phil's day pack",
  "photo": "https://example.com/photo.jpg"
}
```

PDS raises `pds:profile_updated` with a `_status` of `"success"` or `"failure"`.

```krl
rule on_profile_updated {
  select when pds profile_updated
  pre {
    name = event:attr("name")
    status = event:attr("_status")
  }
  if status == "success" then send_directive("profile saved", {"name": name})
}
```

On a thing or a community, you're setting that pico's identity, not its owner's. To change a person's contact details, write to the owner's pico.

### General data

Data is organized by namespace and key. Values can be anything, including maps. Use namespaces so apps don't collide (`safeandmine`, `sensor`, …).

Add or replace an item with `pds:new_data_available`. PDS raises `pds:data_added`:

```krl
raise pds event "new_data_available" attributes {
  "namespace": "safeandmine",
  "key": "contact",
  "value": {"email": "owner@example.com", "phone": "555-0100", "shareEmail": false}
}
```

Merge into a map item with `pds:updated_data_available`, whose `value` is the keys to change. PDS raises `pds:data_updated`:

```krl
raise pds event "updated_data_available" attributes {
  "namespace": "safeandmine",
  "key": "contact",
  "value": {"phone": "555-0199"}
}
```

Replace a whole namespace with `pds:map_item`, whose `mapvalues` is JSON-encoded. PDS raises `pds:new_map_added`:

```krl
raise pds event "map_item" attributes {
  "namespace": "safeandmine",
  "mapvalues": {"tag1": "eci-abc", "tag2": "eci-def"}.encode()
}
```

Remove one item with `pds:remove_old_data` (`namespace`, `key`), which raises `pds:data_deleted`, or a whole namespace with `pds:remove_namespace` (`namespace`), which raises `pds:namespace_deleted`.

### Settings

Settings are keyed by rid. Each entry has a `name`, the `rid`, a `data` map, and an optional `schema`. `pds:add_settings` sets one value, and PDS raises `pds:settings_added`:

```krl
raise pds event "add_settings" attributes {
  "name": "SafeAndMine",
  "keyed_rid": "io.picolabs.safeandmine",
  "schema": [],
  "data_key": "shareEmail",
  "value": true
}
```

### Reacting to changes

| Event | Raised when |
|-------|-------------|
| `pds:data_added` | An item was added |
| `pds:data_updated` | An item was merged into |
| `pds:data_deleted` | An item was removed |
| `pds:namespace_deleted` | A namespace was removed |
| `pds:new_map_added` | A namespace was replaced |
| `pds:profile_updated` | The profile changed |
| `pds:settings_added` | A settings entry changed |

```krl
rule contact_changed {
  select when pds data_updated
    where event:attr("namespace") == "safeandmine" && event:attr("keyvalue") == "contact"
  always {
    raise safeandmine event "contact_changed" attributes event:attrs
  }
}
```

### Clearing everything

`pds:clear_all_data` erases the profile, all general data, and all settings, with no confirmation. It is for tests and developer tools. When an app is uninstalled, remove only its namespace and its settings; the profile should usually stay.

## An example: an app on a thing pico

A lost-and-found app keeps its contact card in general data, uses the profile for the thing's name, and reads share flags from settings. Both `io.picolabs.pds` and the app are installed on the thing pico.

Save the card, through PDS:

```krl
rule information_update {
  select when safeandmine update
  pre {
    card = {
      "email": event:attr("email").defaultsTo("").substr(0, 100),
      "phone": event:attr("phone").defaultsTo("").substr(0, 100),
      "message": event:attr("message").defaultsTo("").substr(0, 250),
      "shareName": event:attr("shareName").as("Boolean").defaultsTo(false),
      "shareEmail": event:attr("shareEmail").as("Boolean").defaultsTo(false)
    }
  }
  always {
    raise pds event "new_data_available" attributes {"namespace": "safeandmine", "key": "contact", "value": card}
  }
}
```

Read the public view of it, combining the profile and the card:

```krl
rule get_information {
  select when safeandmine information_requested
  pre {
    card = pds:items("safeandmine", "contact"){"general"}.defaultsTo({})
    profileName = pds:profile("name"){"profile"}
    result = card.put("name", card{"shareName"} => profileName | null)
  }
  send_directive("contact info", result)
}
```

A notification uses the profile's name, not a copy in the app:

```krl
rule notify {
  select when safeandmine tag_scanned
  pre {
    thingName = pds:profile("name"){"profile"}
    tagID = event:attr("tagID")
  }
  if tagID && thingName then
    event:send({
      "eci": owner_eci,
      "domain": "notification",
      "type": "added",
      "attrs": {"thing": thingName, "message": "Your tag " + tagID + " has been scanned"}
    })
}
```

## The data model

Only PDS rules write these three entity variables.

`ent:profile` is one map per pico. A thing's:

```json
{
  "name": "Blue Backpack",
  "description": "Phil's hiking pack",
  "photo": "https://…",
  "_created": "20260609T120000+0000",
  "_modified": "20260609T153000+0000"
}
```

An owner's might also have `email` and `phone`. Any pico can have those fields.

`ent:general` is a tree of namespaces and keys:

```
"safeandmine"
  "contact"      → { email, phone, message, shareName, … }
  "registry_eci" → "<channel eci>"
"sensor"
  "last_reading" → { … }
```

In KRL, a path into it is `ent:general{[namespace, key]}`.

`ent:settings` is keyed by rid:

```json
{
  "io.picolabs.safeandmine": {
    "name": "SafeAndMine",
    "rid": "io.picolabs.safeandmine",
    "data": {"shareEmail": false, "threshold": 60},
    "schema": []
  }
}
```

Use predictable namespaces so apps coexist on one pico: the framework's (`manifold`), an app's (`safeandmine`), a domain's (`sensor`), or a ruleset's rid.

Don't store secrets in PDS general data unless the channels that can query it are restricted. Channel ECIs are capabilities; treat them as sensitive.

## The protocol

Writing:

1. An app's ruleset raises a `pds` event (`updated_profile`, `new_data_available`, …).
2. A PDS rule checks the attributes and updates its entity variable.
3. PDS raises a notification event (`profile_updated`, `data_added`, …) on the same pico.
4. Other rulesets select the notification to react.

Apps never assign `ent:profile`, `ent:general`, or `ent:settings` themselves, which keeps storage in one place.

Reading: on the same pico, use the ruleset as a module; from another pico, `wrangler:picoQuery(eci, "io.picolabs.pds", function, params)` on a channel that allows it.

| | Relationships | PDS |
|-|---------------|-----|
| Problem | Communication between picos | Data storage within a pico |
| Mechanism | Channels and the relationship ruleset | Events and shared queries |
| Identity | `Tx`, `Rx`, roles | Profile name, namespaces |
| Installed | On every pico | On every pico |

```
App ruleset                PDS                         Other rulesets on the pico
  |-- pds:updated_profile -->|                                    |
  |                          |-- merge ent:profile                |
  |                          |-- pds:profile_updated ------------>| (if they select it)
```

## Security

PDS is a data contract, not an authorization layer.

Entity variables belong to their ruleset, so another ruleset's `ent:contactInfo` is a different variable and can't overwrite PDS storage. Other rulesets reach PDS data by reading through the module or `picoQuery`, and by writing with `pds` events, which only PDS rules handle.

| Layer | Mechanism | What it protects |
|-------|-----------|------------------|
| Access from other picos | ECI and channel policy | Remote events and queries, including PDS queries |
| What runs on the pico | Who installs rulesets | Which rulesets run |
| Writes from the same pico | None today | — |

Any ruleset installed on a pico can raise `pds:updated_profile`, `pds:new_data_available`, `pds:clear_all_data`, and the rest. PDS doesn't check which ruleset raised them (it uses `meta:callingRID()` for settings reads, not for writes). So security depends on trusting every ruleset installed on the pico. Other picos need a channel that allows `pds` events or `io.picolabs.pds` queries; that's uncommon for writes.

Practical guidance:

- Install only rulesets you trust on production picos.
- Use namespaces consistently, so apps don't duplicate canonical data.
- Restrict query channels when general data includes sensitive fields.
- Treat `pds:clear_all_data` as destructive.

### Planned

- Write authorization: checking `meta:callingRID()` on writes, so only the owning app writes its namespace.
- Engine-level workload identity and policy before events reach rulesets.
- Channel templates and install allowlists that limit what application rulesets can declare.

## See also

- [Relationships](/wrangler/relationships): channels between picos, and roles
- [Managing channels](/wrangler/channels): ECIs and channel policies


---

# Wrangler: pico views (io.picolabs.xmlui)

# Pico views: io.picolabs.xmlui

*Optional. Not installed by default. Install it on each pico that serves pages.*

`io.picolabs.xmlui` lets a pico serve web pages built with [XMLUI](https://xmlui.org). A ruleset function tagged `@view` is a page, at `/ui/<eci>/<rid>/`. One tagged `@component` is a reusable part that pages use as a tag. This ruleset supplies the app shell and navigation, the helpers a view uses to read and write the pico, and shared components: `PicoTheme`, `PicoSettings`, `PicoThemeField`, and `PicoAccessTokenField`.

## Install it

From a pico's **Rulesets** tab, install it from the engine:

```
http://localhost:3000/krl/io.picolabs.xmlui.krl
```

Or from a ruleset, the way the Try It! demos' bootstraps do:

```krl
raise wrangler event "install_ruleset_request" attributes {"url": meta:host + "/krl/io.picolabs.xmlui.krl"}
```

Install it before the rulesets that use it as a module.

## Use it

```krl
meta {
  use module io.picolabs.xmlui alias ui
  shares hello
}
global {
  /**
   * A greeting.
   * @view "Hello"
   */
  hello = function() {
    <<
<Component name="Hello">
  <Text>Hello from #{meta:rid}</Text>
</Component>
>>
  }
}
```

Its main helpers:

| Helper | Use |
|--------|-----|
| `ui:query_url(name, rid, eci)`, `ui:event_url(domain, type, eci)` | URLs for a page's `DataSource` and `APICall` |
| `ui:query(id, name, opts)`, `ui:event(id, domain, type, opts)` | The `DataSource` and `APICall` markup itself. Pass `{"rid": meta:rid}` to `ui:query` |
| `ui:create_app_channel(tags, domains, queries, rid)` | A channel for the app: events in `domains`, its queries, and what the page shell needs |
| `ui:rotate_app_channel(tags)` | A new channel like the newest one with those tags |
| `ui:app_url(tags, rid)` | The page's URL on the newest channel with those tags |

When a pico's set of rulesets changes, this ruleset adds any missing component queries to the channels that serve pages.

## Read more

- [Pico views](/pico-views): the full guide, including channels, components, and OAuth meshes.
- The [Pico views demos](/cookbook/xmlui/), and every Try It! demo, which all use it.


---

# Wrangler: OAuth (io.picolabs.oauth)

# OAuth: io.picolabs.oauth

*Optional. Not installed by default. Install it on the root pico only. API reference: [io.picolabs.oauth](/rulesets/io.picolabs.oauth).*

`io.picolabs.oauth` turns on OAuth for a mesh: once it is installed on the mesh's root pico, most requests to `/sky/*` need an access token (a bearer token). It also holds the mesh's OAuth configuration.

Without it, a channel's policy is the only gate on `/sky/*`: anyone with the ECI can use what the policy allows. The developer UI and the engine's own calls use passkey sessions on `/c/*`, and OAuth doesn't change that.

## Install it

On the root pico's **Rulesets** tab, install `https://<your engine>/krl/io.picolabs.oauth.krl`. To turn OAuth off for the mesh again, uninstall it.

## What needs a token

| Channel | Needs a bearer token on `/sky/*`? |
|---------|-----------------------------------|
| Tagged `didcomm` and `ingress` | No: DIDComm traffic between engines |
| Tagged `oauth-webhook` | Yes, always, even without this ruleset |
| Tagged `mesh-oauth-exempt` | No: opts out of the mesh lock |
| Any other, with this ruleset on the root | Yes |
| Any other, without it | No |

Use `mesh-oauth-exempt` for webhook channels whose senders can't add an `Authorization` header. Their event policy still applies. If a channel has both `oauth-webhook` and `mesh-oauth-exempt`, `oauth-webhook` wins.

## Two kinds of credentials

| Grant | For | Client id | Reaches |
|-------|-----|-----------|---------|
| Client credentials | Incoming webhooks (from services such as GitHub or Stripe) | The channel's ECI | That one channel |
| Authorization code with PKCE | Apps such as Home Assistant | `app_…` | The whole mesh |

**Webhook credentials.** Tag a channel `oauth-webhook`. On the **Channels** tab, create credentials for it: the client id is the ECI, and the secret is shown once. Exchange them for a token at `POST /oauth/token` with `grant_type` `client_credentials`. The token (`oat_…`) works only on `/sky/*` for that ECI. Family, relationship, and system channels can't have credentials.

**Apps.** With this ruleset installed, register an app under **Settings** → **OAuth apps**, with its redirect URIs. The app sends the user to `/oauth/authorize`, the user approves with their passkey, and the app exchanges the code for tokens at `/oauth/token`.

## From KRL

The ruleset shares functions for the mesh's state, for rulesets on the root pico:

| Function | Returns |
|----------|---------|
| `meshEnabled()` | Whether OAuth is on for this mesh |
| `meshRequiresOAuth(eci)` | Whether a request on that channel needs a token |
| `channelStatus(eci)` | A channel's OAuth status |
| `createChannelSecret(eci)`, `revokeChannelSecret(eci)`, `revokeTokens(eci)` | Manage a webhook channel's credentials |

Creating a new channel secret revokes the tokens already made from the old one.

## Effects elsewhere

- [Pico views](/pico-views) on an OAuth mesh need an access token in the browser; see their OAuth section.
- The Try It! demos aren't meant for OAuth meshes: their pages send no token.
- The mesh MCP server (`/mcp/:eci`) needs a bearer token.

The package README's OAuth section has the HTTP details for every grant.


---

# Wrangler: portable subtrees (io.picolabs.portable_subtree)

# Portable subtrees: io.picolabs.portable_subtree

*Optional. Not installed by default. API reference: [io.picolabs.portable_subtree](/rulesets/io.picolabs.portable_subtree).*

`io.picolabs.portable_subtree` copies a pico and all its descendants to another parent, on the same engine or on another one. It copies their rulesets, entity state, channels, schedules, and identity. Each pico keeps its `did:webvh`, and its DID-based relationships are moved so they keep working.

## Export

Install it on an ancestor of the pico you want to copy (the root pico works). Then query it:

```krl
blob = portable_subtree:exportSubtree(subtree_root_pico_id, secret)
```

The result is an encrypted blob. Move it to the destination however you like. Keep the secret separately: it isn't in the blob.

## Inspect

Before importing, check what a blob holds, with the same secret:

```krl
portable_subtree:summarizeExportBlob(blob, secret)
```

## Import

Install the ruleset on the pico that will be the new parent, and send it:

```krl
raise portable_subtree event "import" attributes {"blob": blob, "secret": secret}
```

The subtree becomes a child of that pico. The ruleset raises `portable_subtree:imported`, and `portable_subtree:lastImport()` returns the result. Wrangler on the imported pico raises `wrangler:subtree_imported`.

## Things to know

- **What the subtree relied on.** Picos often depend on services their ancestors provide: shared rulesets, relationships to a framework's picos, channels set up by a parent. The new parent has to provide them too. For example, import a Manifold app's pico under a Manifold parent, not under a bare root.
- **The original stays.** Exporting copies; it doesn't remove anything. Delete the source subtree yourself when you no longer need it.
- **The blob is sensitive.** It holds the subtree's state and capabilities. Treat it, and its secret, like credentials.

## Read more

- The [Moving picos](/cookbook/moving_picos/) demo: export a pico and its children from one engine and import them on another.
- [The design of pico moves](/design/pico-move).


---

# Patterns and tips

# Patterns and tips

Short techniques for writing KRL and running picos, checked against the current engine. They come from the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook, which was written for earlier engines. The pages here have been updated where KRL or the engine has changed. For runnable examples, see the [Cookbook](/cookbook/) and the developer UI's **Try It!** tab.

## Working with data

| Page | What it covers |
|------|----------------|
| [Initializing entity variables](/patterns_and_tips/initializing-entity-variables) | `defaultsTo`, a guard rule, or a rule that runs on install |
| [Arrays and maps](/patterns_and_tips/arrays-and-maps) | Loops with `reduce`, flattening, and sorting arrays of maps by one key or two |
| [Decoding form-encoded data](/patterns_and_tips/decoding-form-data) | Turning `a=1&b=2` into a map, keeping repeated names, and decoding `+` and `%xx` |
| [Importing tables and CSV](/patterns_and_tips/tabular-data) | Tab- and comma-separated exports to arrays and maps, fetched with `http:get` |
| [Converting time formats](/patterns_and_tips/converting-time-formats) | RSS (RFC 2822) dates to the RFC 3339 form the time library uses |
| [What's in a name?](/patterns_and_tips/names-and-scope) | KRL's separate kinds of names, and how a `pre` declaration shadows a global |

## HTTP and the outside world

| Page | What it covers |
|------|----------------|
| [Events and queries over HTTP](/patterns_and_tips/events-and-queries-over-http) | Event and query URLs, `curl`, POST bodies, `.txt` and `.html` results, and `_headers` |
| [Cookies and redirects](/patterns_and_tips/cookies-and-redirects) | The `_cookie` and `_redirect` directives, reading cookies, and a URL shortener |

| [Reading the engine's log files](/patterns_and_tips/engine-log-files) | Where the logs are, how they rotate, and one pico's history with `grep` and `jq` |

## Picos working together

| Page | What it covers |
|------|----------------|
| [Querying another pico](/patterns_and_tips/querying-another-pico) | `wrangler:picoQuery`, which channel to use, why a pico can't query itself, and `http:get` |
| [Accepting relationship requests](/patterns_and_tips/accepting-relationship-requests) | An approving rule, wrangler's auto-accept configuration, and a ruleset that accepts later and removes itself |
| [One pico per resource](/patterns_and_tips/singleton-picos) | Giving a device or account its own pico, so requests can't collide |

## Developing rulesets

## Left out

Pages that describe things the current engine no longer has, or that depend on outside services:

- **Sending secure messages** used `engine:signChannelMessage` and its relatives, which are gone. Relationships between picos can use DIDComm now; see the [`dido` library](/krl/libraries/dido/).
- **Shorter URL for a query or event** used `io.picolabs.rewrite` on the root pico, removed in engine 1.0. A ruleset can do the same with `_redirect`: see [Cookies and redirects](/patterns_and_tips/cookies-and-redirects).
- **Account management using the root pico** described owner picos from before engine 1.0.
- **Generate an image with KRL**, **Using Foursquare data**, **Using Wovyn sensors**, **Using Git**, and **Using a Google sheet** are about particular services, devices, or tools rather than KRL.
- **Proposals, experiments, and proofs of concept** (personal channels, generating KRL with KRL, JavaScript rulesets, and others) were experiments on earlier engines.

# Tip: initializing entity variables

# Initializing entity variables

Each ruleset installed in a pico gives the pico its own entity variables, specific to that pico and that ruleset. Until a rule's postlude first assigns one, its value is `null`. There are three ways to deal with that.

## Use `defaultsTo` wherever you read it

`defaultsTo` supplies a value when the variable is `null`. Suppose `ent:owners` will be a map but might not exist yet:

```krl
nameExists = function(ownername) {
  ent:owners.defaultsTo({}) >< ownername
}
```

The first time the map is stored, start from the same default:

```krl
rule owner_token {
  select when owner token_created
  pre {
    name = event:attr("name")
    new_owner = event:attr("owner")
  }
  fired {
    ent:owners := ent:owners.defaultsTo({}).put(name, new_owner)
  }
}
```

With this technique, every use of `ent:owners` in the ruleset needs `defaultsTo`. A shared function that returns `ent:owners.defaultsTo({})` keeps that in one place.

## Initialize it in a guard rule

Put a rule before the others that select the same event, and have it create the variable when it is missing:

```krl
rule guard_owners_map {
  select when owner token_created
  if ent:owners.isnull() then noop()
  fired {
    ent:owners := {}
  }
}
```

Rules in one ruleset that select the same event run in the order they are written, so this one runs first. The rules after it can then use a path assignment, which is also faster for a large map:

```krl
rule owner_token {
  select when owner token_created
  pre {
    name = event:attr("name")
    new_owner = event:attr("owner")
  }
  fired {
    ent:owners{name} := new_owner
  }
}
```

Functions still need `defaultsTo`, in case a query arrives before any event does.

## Initialize it when the ruleset is installed

A rule that selects the ruleset's own `wrangler:ruleset_installed` runs before anything else can use the ruleset:

```krl
rule initialization {
  select when wrangler ruleset_installed where event:attr("rids") >< meta:rid
  if ent:owners.isnull() then noop()
  fired {
    ent:owners := {}
  }
}
```

The `where` clause matters. Many rulesets are installed in a pico over its life, and without it this rule would run every time. Checking `isnull()` first is good practice too.

Installing again from the same URL, or flushing, does not raise `ruleset_installed` again. A rule like this runs once per install.

See also: [Persistent variables](/krl/persistent-variables/) in the KRL manual, and the [Guard rules](/cookbook/guard_rules/) demo.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Initializing entity variables".*


---

# Tip: arrays and maps

# Arrays and maps

KRL has no `for` loop in expressions. Array operators do the same work: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `sort`, and the others in [Array operators](/krl/krl-expression-language/operators/array-operators). Here are a few patterns that come up often.

## Loop with `reduce`

To repeat a step a fixed number of times, `reduce` over a range and carry the state in the accumulator. This converts a number to an 8-byte array, high byte first, the way this JavaScript does:

```js
for (var index = 0; index < byteArray.length; index++) {
  var byte = long & 0xff;
  byteArray[index] = byte;
  long = (long - byte) / 256;
}
```

```krl
toByteArray = function(str) {
  1.range(8)
    .reduce(function(a, i) {
      [a[0].append(a[1] % 256), math:int(a[1] / 256)]
    }, [[], str.as("Number")])
    .head()
    .reverse()
}
```

`1.range(8)` is `[1, 2, ... 8]`. It only counts; the function doesn't use `i`. The accumulator is a pair: the bytes so far, and what's left of the number. Each step appends the low byte and divides by 256. At the end, `head()` takes the bytes and `reverse()` puts the high byte first. `toByteArray("1551127401")` is `[0,0,0,0,92,116,83,105]`.

Add `.klog("step")` inside the function to watch the accumulator change on each step.

The inverse is one `reduce`. With no initial value, it starts from the first element:

```krl
fromByteArray = function(bytes) {
  bytes.reduce(function(a, b) { a * 256 + b })
}
```

## Flatten an array of arrays

```krl
[[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8, 9]].reduce(function(a, b) { a.append(b) }, [])
// [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
```

## Sort an array of maps

`sort` takes a comparison function. A function that returns one, for a given key, reads well:

```krl
by = function(key) {
  function(a, b) { a{key}.encode() cmp b{key}.encode() }
}
```

`wrangler:channels().sort(by("id"))` reads "my channels, sorted by id". `cmp` compares strings, and `encode()` turns any value into a string, so `by` works whatever the values are. For numbers, compare them as numbers instead: `people.sort(function(a, b) { a{"born"} <=> b{"born"} })`.

For a primary and a secondary key:

```krl
by = function(key1, key2) {
  key2 =>
    function(a, b) {
      a{key1}.encode() cmp b{key1}.encode() ||
      a{key2}.encode() cmp b{key2}.encode()
    }
  |
    function(a, b) { a{key1}.encode() cmp b{key1}.encode() }
}
```

`||` stops at the first comparison that isn't zero, so the second key only breaks ties. `by("last", "first")` sorts by last name, then first name, and `by` still works with one key.

A key can also be a path, such as `by(["meta", "flushed"])`, because `a{["meta", "flushed"]}` looks up a nested value.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook pages "Looping using the reduce operator", "Flatten an Array of Arrays", and "Sorting an Array of Maps".*

# Tip: decoding form-encoded data

# Decoding form-encoded data

Form-encoded content, such as `q=5&value=%20space%20`, sometimes arrives as a single string: in a webhook body, a stored URL, or a query string you built. A chain of operators turns it into a map.

## Names and values

```krl
nv_split = function(x) { x.extract(re#([^=]*)=?(.*)#) }  // "n=v" -> ["n", "v"]
frst = function(a) { a.head() }
dup_1st = function(v) { v[0][1] }

decodeContent = function(content) {
  content            // "n0=v0&n1=v1&..."
    .split(re#&#)    // ["n0=v0", "n1=v1", ...]
    .map(nv_split)   // [["n0", "v0"], ["n1", "v1"], ...]
    .collect(frst)   // {"n0": [["n0", "v0"]], "n1": [["n1", "v1"]], ...}
    .map(dup_1st)    // {"n0": "v0", "n1": "v1", ...}
}
```

`decodeContent("q=5&value=%20space%20")` is `{"q": "5", "value": "%20space%20"}`.

- `split` makes an array of `name=value` strings.
- `extract` matches each one against a regular expression and returns its capture groups, the name and the value.
- `collect` groups the pairs into a map keyed by name. Each value is an array of every pair with that name.
- The map operator `map` keeps the first value for each name.

## Keep every value of a repeated name

When a name can repeat, keep all its values:

```krl
dup_all = function(v) {
  v.length() == 1 => v[0][1] | v.map(function(w) { w[1] })
}
```

Use `.map(dup_all)` in place of `.map(dup_1st)`. `a=1&a=2&b=3` becomes `{"a": ["1", "2"], "b": "3"}`.

## Decode `+` and `%xx`

`replace` accepts a function as its second argument. It is called with the match and then each capture group, and returns the replacement:

```krl
hexDigits = "0123456789abcdef"

hex2dec = function(hex) {
  hex like re#^[0-9A-Fa-f]+$#
    => hex.lc().split("").reduce(function(a, h) { a * 16 + hexDigits.split("").index(h) }, 0)
    | null
}

hex2char = function(encoded, hex) {
  val = hex2dec(hex)
  val && val < 128 => val.chr() | encoded
}

decode_val = function(s) {
  s.replace(re#[+]#g, " ").replace(re#%([0-9A-Fa-f]{2})#g, hex2char)
}
```

Replace `+` first: early encoders used it for a space, and a real plus sign arrives as `%2B`. Then use `function(v) { decode_val(v[0][1]) }` as the last step of the chain. `value=%20space%20&plus=a%2Bb&pct=100%25` becomes `{"value": " space ", "plus": "a+b", "pct": "100%"}`. This handles ASCII characters. Anything above 127 is left encoded.

Events and queries that arrive over HTTP are already decoded: the engine gives you their attributes as a map. This is for strings you have in hand.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Decoding WWW-Form Encoded Content or Query Parameters".*


---

# Tip: importing tables and CSV

# Importing tables and CSV

Data exported from a spreadsheet or another system usually arrives as text: tab-separated (TSV) or comma-separated (CSV) lines. If the other system can export JSON, use that instead. `decode()` turns a JSON string into KRL data in one step.

## Lines

Exports end lines with `\n` or, from Windows, `\r\n`. One regular expression handles both:

```krl
lineBreak = re#\r?\n#
lines = content.split(lineBreak).filter(function(s) { s })
```

`filter(function(s) { s })` drops empty lines: an empty string is falsy, and there is usually one after the last line break. Another way is to let a global regular expression find the lines: `content.extract(re#(.+)#g)`.

## A table to an array of maps

When the first row names the columns, make each data row a map:

```krl
tsv = function(content) {
  lines = content.split(re#\r?\n#).filter(function(s) { s })
  keys = lines.head().split(re#\t#)
  lines.tail().map(function(line) {
    values = line.split(re#\t#)
    keys.reduce(function(m, k, i) { m.put(k, values[i]) }, {})
  })
}
```

Given

```
A	B
1	2
3	4
```

`tsv(content)` is `[{"A": "1", "B": "2"}, {"A": "3", "B": "4"}]`. The `reduce` passes each key's index as its third argument, which picks the matching value.

## CSV with a known shape

CSV is harder, because a value that contains a comma is wrapped in double quotes. When you know what each line looks like, match the whole line with a regular expression and let the last group take the rest:

```krl
graduands = function(content) {
  content.extract(re#(.+)#g)
    .tail()
    .map(function(line) { line.extract(re#^([\w ]+),(\w+),(\d+),(\d+),(.*)$#) })
}
```

`Ada Lovelace,AL,1,1843,"Notes, on the engine"` becomes `["Ada Lovelace", "AL", "1", "1843", "\"Notes, on the engine\""]`. Strip the quotes from that last field if you need to. `tail()` skips the header line.

## Fetch the file

Rather than passing a whole file to a function, give it a URL:

```krl
import = function(url) {
  tsv(http:get(url){"content"})
}
```

A function that calls `http:get` runs on every query, so for a large file, import it once in a rule and store the result in an entity variable.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook pages "Converting a table to an Array of Maps" and "Importing data from other systems".*

# Tip: converting time formats

# Converting time formats

The [time library](/krl/libraries/time) works with ISO 8601 / RFC 3339 times such as `2011-09-21T15:02:01-07:00`. Other formats need converting first. RSS feeds, for example, give dates like `Wed, 21 Sep 2011 15:02:01 -0700` (RFC 2822), and `time:new` rejects them: `time:new was given an invalid date string`.

This function rearranges the parts:

```krl
mon2num = {
  "Jan": "01", "Feb": "02", "Mar": "03", "Apr": "04", "May": "05", "Jun": "06",
  "Jul": "07", "Aug": "08", "Sep": "09", "Oct": "10", "Nov": "11", "Dec": "12"
}

rss2krlTime = function(pubDate) {
  tarr = pubDate.split(re# #)
  tzoff = tarr[5].replace(re#(\d\d)$#, ":$1")
  tarr[3] + "-" + mon2num{tarr[2]} + "-" + tarr[1] + "T" + tarr[4] + tzoff
}
```

`split` gives `["Wed,", "21", "Sep", "2011", "15:02:01", "-0700"]`. The offset `-0700` becomes `-07:00`, and `+0530` becomes `+05:30`. Then the time library can format it:

```krl
time:strftime(rss2krlTime("Wed, 21 Sep 2011 15:02:01 -0700"), "%b %d %Y")   // "Sep 21 2011"
```

This expects a two-digit day, as RSS feeds use. For a feed that writes `1 Sep`, pad the day first, for example with `tarr[1].length() == 1 => "0" + tarr[1] | tarr[1]`.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Converting Time Formats" (originally by Ed Orcutt). The time-zone handling here also covers offsets that aren't whole hours.*


---

# Tip: what's in a name

# What's in a name?

KRL keeps many kinds of names apart: the ruleset id, rule names, event domains and types, attribute names, global and local names, function parameters, and directive names. As an exercise, here is a ruleset where every one of them is `name`:

```krl
ruleset name {
  meta {
    shares name
  }
  global {
    /**
     * @param name String
     */
    name = function(name) {
      name.klog("name") => name | "name"
    }
  }
  rule name {
    select when name name
    pre {
      name = event:attr("name").defaultsTo(name(name), "name")
    }
    send_directive("name", {"name": name || "name"})
  }
  rule name_provided {
    select when name name name re#(.+)# setting(name)
    send_directive("name", {"name": name})
  }
}
```

It works. Most of the uses can't collide: an event domain, a rule name, and a directive name live in different places. One line is worth a closer look:

```krl
name = event:attr("name").defaultsTo(name(name), "name")
```

The right-hand side is evaluated before the binding. At that moment `name` is still the global function, so `name(name)` calls the function with itself as the argument, and it returns itself, because a function is truthy. After the line, `name` is bound to the result, and the global function is shadowed for the rest of the rule.

Raise `name:name` with `name` set to `Ada` and both rules answer `{"name": "Ada"}`. Raise it without the attribute and `defaultsTo` uses the function (logging `"name"`). The directive's `name` is then a function, which doesn't survive conversion to JSON, so the reply shows `{}`.

So: a name declared in `pre` hides a global of the same name for the rest of that rule. That is legal, and usually a mistake. And a name in `pre` can't be declared twice. KRL declarations are not assignments.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "What's in a name?".*


---

# Tip: events and queries over HTTP

# Events and queries over HTTP

A pico's events and queries are plain HTTP, so anything that can make a request can talk to a pico: `curl`, a browser, a script, a webhook from another service.

## Raise an event

```
/sky/event/<eci>/<eid>/<domain>/<type>?<attributes>
```

- `<eci>` is a channel on the pico. Its event policy has to allow `<domain>:<type>`. Make channels on the pico's **Channels** tab, or have a ruleset create one when it is installed (see the [Bootstrap and channels](/cookbook/bootstrap/) demo).
- `<eid>` is an event id of your choosing, for your own tracing. Anything works; `none` is common.
- Attributes go in the query string, or in a POST body (form-encoded or JSON). When both have the same name, the body wins.

```sh
curl "http://localhost:3000/sky/event/<eci>/none/echo/message?input=hello"

curl -X POST "http://localhost:3000/sky/event/<eci>/none/echo/message" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"input": "hello"}'
```

The response is JSON with the `directives` the rules sent and `ruleOutcomes`, which say which rules fired. A channel that doesn't allow the event answers `{"error":"Error: Not allowed by channel policy"}`.

## Ask a query

```
/sky/cloud/<eci>/<rid>/<function>?<arguments>
```

The function has to be shared by the ruleset, and allowed by the channel's query policy. The answer is the function's value, as JSON.

## Get text or HTML instead of JSON

Add `.txt` or `.html` to the function name and the engine returns the string the function produced, with that content type:

```krl
page = function() {
  <<<h1>Hello from a pico</h1>
>>
}
```

`/sky/cloud/<eci>/<rid>/page.html` shows a heading in a browser. `/sky/cloud/<eci>/<rid>/page.txt` shows the markup as text. For whole pages, use a [pico view](/pico-views) instead.

## See the request

Every event raised over HTTP has an attribute `_headers` with the request's HTTP headers, and every query has an argument by the same name. See [Cookies and redirects](/patterns_and_tips/cookies-and-redirects) for one use.

## From the developer UI

On a pico's **Testing** tab, pick a ruleset and fill in the form for any documented event or query, then send it on the channel you choose. Documented means it has a doc comment: the Testing tab builds its forms from the ruleset's schema.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook pages "Raising Events" and "Content negotiation with HTTP".*


---

# Tip: cookies and redirects

# Cookies and redirects

Two directive names are special. When a rule sends one in response to an event raised over HTTP, the engine turns it into part of the HTTP response.

## Set a cookie: `_cookie`

```krl
rule set_cookie {
  select when cookie needed
  pre {
    eci = wrangler:channels(["wellKnown_Rx", "Tx_Rx"]).head(){"id"} || meta:eci
  }
  send_directive("_cookie", {"cookie": <<wellKnown_Rx=#{eci}; Path=/sky>>})
}
```

The engine adds `Set-Cookie: wellKnown_Rx=<eci>; Path=/sky` to the response, and the browser sends the cookie back with later requests to the same engine. This one shares the pico's well-known channel, so other picos reached from the same browser could offer it a relationship. The ruleset uses `io.picolabs.wrangler` as a module.

## Read cookies

Every event raised over HTTP has a `_headers` attribute, and every query a `_headers` argument. This function works in both:

```krl
cookies = function(_headers) {
  arg = event:attr("_headers") || _headers
  arg{"cookie"}.isnull() => {} |
  arg{"cookie"}
    .split("; ")
    .map(function(v) { v.split("=") })
    .collect(function(v) { v.head() })
    .map(function(v) { v.head()[1] })
}
```

With the header `Cookie: wellKnown_Rx=abc123; sessionid=38afes7a8`, `cookies()` is `{"wellKnown_Rx": "abc123", "sessionid": "38afes7a8"}`. The chain is the same idea as [decoding form data](/patterns_and_tips/decoding-form-data), splitting on `"; "` instead of `&`.

## Redirect: `_redirect`

```krl
send_directive("_redirect", {"url": "https://picolabs.io/"})
```

The engine answers the event with HTTP 302 and that URL as the `Location`.

## A URL shortener

Together with a channel per link, `_redirect` makes a URL shortener. Each link gets its own channel, whose policy allows only the event that follows it. The channel id is the short URL:

```krl
ruleset s {
  meta {
    use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
    provides u
  }
  global {
    u = function(eci) {
      <<#{meta:host}/sky/event/#{eci}/none/s/u>>
    }
  }
  rule recordShortcut {
    select when s u
      url re#(.+)# setting(url)
    pre {
      tag = event:attr("tag").lc().replace(re#[^a-z0-9_.-]#g, "-")
      eid = tag => tag | "none"
    }
    every {
      wrangler:createChannel(
        [eid, "s"],
        {"allow": [{"domain": "s", "name": "u"}], "deny": []},
        {"allow": [], "deny": [{"rid": "*", "name": "*"}]}
      ) setting(channel)
      send_directive("shortcut registered", {"tag": tag, "eci": channel{"id"}, "shortcut": u(channel{"id"}), "url": url})
    }
    fired {
      ent:shortcuts{channel{"id"}} := url
    }
  }
  rule redirectShortcut {
    select when s u
      where event:attr("url").isnull()
    send_directive("_redirect", {"url": ent:shortcuts{meta:eci}})
  }
}
```

Another ruleset uses it as a module. It registers a link with `raise s event "u" attributes {"url": long_url, "tag": "docs"}`, then finds the channel with `wrangler:channels(["docs", "s"]).head()` and the short form with `s:u(eci)`. Opening the short URL redirects to the long one. The short URL can only raise `s:u`, and queries on it are all denied. Short links are handy in QR codes, which get smaller as the URL does.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook pages "Setting and reading cookies" and "Ruleset that provides a general purpose URL shortener".*


---

# Tip: events from email

# Events from email

Any service that can call a webhook can raise events on a pico. Email is a good example: services such as [CloudMailin](https://www.cloudmailin.com/) give you an address and POST each message that arrives to a URL you choose. Point that URL at a pico:

```
https://<your engine>/sky/event/<eci>/mail/mail/received
```

The engine has to be reachable from the internet. For an engine on your own machine, a tunnel such as [ngrok](https://ngrok.com/) gives it a public address. Use a channel made for this purpose, whose policy allows only `mail:received`, so the webhook URL can't do anything else.

## Parse the message

The service's POST body becomes the event's attributes. With CloudMailin's JSON format, the headers and the plain-text body are in `headers` and `plain`:

```krl
rule mail_incoming {
  select when mail received
  pre {
    headers = event:attr("headers").defaultsTo({})
  }
  always {
    raise mail event "parsed" attributes {
      "date": headers{"Date"},
      "to": headers{"To"},
      "from": headers{"From"},
      "subject": headers{"Subject"},
      "text": event:attr("plain")
    }
  }
}
```

## Route it to another pico

One mail pico can serve many. Put the target pico's channel id in the address, as in `me+<eci>@cloudmailin.net`, and forward on it:

```krl
rule mail_router {
  select when mail parsed
    to re#[+]([^@]*)@#
    setting(eci)
  event:send({"eci": eci, "domain": "mail", "type": "events", "attrs": event:attrs})
}
```

The person writing the email needs that address, but not where the target pico lives.

## Turn lines into events

The target pico can treat each line of the body as an event to raise. Here, a line such as `aurora/on` raises `aurora:on`, and every other line is ignored:

```krl
rule mail_events {
  select when mail events
  foreach event:attr("text").defaultsTo("").split(re#\r?\n#) setting(request)
  pre {
    parts = request.split(re#/#)
    wanted = parts.length() == 2 && parts[0] == "aurora"
  }
  if wanted then noop()
  fired {
    raise aurora event parts[1]
  }
}
```

A body of

```
Turn on the lights, then show the second theme after this one.
aurora/on
aurora/next
aurora/next
```

raises `aurora:on` and `aurora:next` twice, which the pico's existing rulesets handle. The new ruleset doesn't change them.

Parsing the body is the fragile part. Email clients add things you don't expect, such as invisible characters. Test with messages from the clients your senders use.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Triggering Events from Email Messages".*


---

# Tip: reading the engine's log files

# Reading the engine's log files

The **Logging** tab shows recent events and queries for a pico, from the engine's memory. To look further back, or across every pico, read the log files.

## Where they are

The engine writes one JSON object per line to `pico-engine.log` in its home directory (`PICO_ENGINE_HOME`, `~/.pico-engine` by default). When the file reaches 100 MB it rotates: the older entries move to `pico-engine.log.1`, `pico-engine.log.2`, and so on, and the engine keeps up to twelve files. `PICO_ENGINE_LOG_FILE` writes somewhere else instead (`stdout` to write to standard output). See [the operator guide](/pico-engine) for the settings.

Each line has `level`, `time`, and `msg`, and lines about a pico's work have `picoId` and `txnId`. A transaction is one event or query and everything it caused.

```json
{"level":50,"time":"2026-11-13T18:46:16.317Z","picoId":"cmwfbv2y1001e4jysd0cn9w05","txnId":"cmwfbvcvx00244jysd16w7grz","txnKind":"query","error":"This is a family channel and only the owner can use it.","msg":"..."}
```

## One pico's history

Find the pico's id on its **About** tab, then:

```sh
cd ~/.pico-engine
grep -h '"picoId":"<pico id>"' pico-engine.log* | jq -s -c 'sort_by(.time)[]' > my_pico.log
```

`grep` collects the lines from every file, and [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/) sorts them by time, since rotated files aren't in order relative to each other. To follow one event through everything it caused, filter on its `txnId` instead.

## What to look for

- `"msg":"txnQueued"` lines show each event or query as it arrived, with its attributes.
- `"error"` fields show what failed: a channel policy refusal, a KRL runtime error, a family channel used from outside.
- `klog` output from your own rules is in the log, with the message you gave it.

The logs hold every event's attributes. Anything secret that arrives in an event is in them. See the [Configuration and secrets](/cookbook/secrets/) demo.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Examining pico-engine log files". The log format and rotation have changed since that page was written.*


---

# Tip: querying another pico

# Querying another pico

To call a function another pico's ruleset shares, use `wrangler:picoQuery`. Two things are needed: a channel to the other pico whose query policy allows that function, and `io.picolabs.wrangler` as a module.

```krl
meta {
  use module io.picolabs.wrangler alias wrangler
}
```

```krl
rule ask_the_other_pico {
  select when example question_asked
  pre {
    answer = wrangler:picoQuery(other_eci, "my.ruleset.id", "myFunction", {"arg1": "a", "arg2": "b"})
  }
  if answer{"error"}.isnull() then noop()
  fired {
    ent:last_answer := answer
  }
}
```

On the same engine, `picoQuery` calls the other pico directly. On another engine, or for a `did:` identifier, it goes over HTTP or DIDComm. Either way it returns the function's value, or a map with an `error` key if something went wrong.

## Which channel

- **Your children.** `wrangler:children()` gives each child's family channel (`eci`). `picoQuery` can use it, because the parent owns it.
- **Picos you have a relationship with.** Use the relationship: `subscription:queryOnSub(Id, rid, name, args)` (see the [Two picos talking](/cookbook/two_picos/) demo), or `picoQuery` on the relationship's `Tx` channel.
- **Anyone else.** A channel they give you, made for the purpose, with a policy that allows the functions you need.

## Don't query yourself

A pico handles one thing at a time. A query from a pico to itself would wait behind the work that's making it. `picoQuery` refuses: it returns `{"status_code": 400, ...}` with the error "Pico should not query itself". To use a function in another ruleset on the same pico, use that ruleset as a module instead.

## With `http:get`

A pico has a URL, so `http:get` works too:

```krl
response = http:get(meta:host + "/sky/cloud/" + other_eci + "/my.ruleset.id/myFunction", {"arg1": "a"})
answer = response{"content"}.decode()
```

It's slower than `picoQuery` on the same engine, and it can't use family channels: the answer is an error, "This is a family channel and only the owner can use it". The HTTP status is still 200 in that case, so check the content for `error`, not just `status_code`.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Accessing a Function Shared by Another Pico".*


---

# Tip: accepting relationship requests

# Accepting relationship requests

When another pico asks for a relationship, the request waits on the receiving pico (its **Relationships** tab lists it) until something approves it. Here are three ways to approve requests automatically. The examples share one setup: a list pico asks participant picos to join it, in the role `participant list` for itself and `participant` for them.

## A rule that approves

On each participant:

```krl
rule accept_list {
  select when wrangler inbound_pending_subscription_added
    where event:attr("Rx_role") == "participant"
       && event:attr("Tx_role") == "participant list"
  always {
    raise wrangler event "pending_subscription_approval" attributes event:attrs
  }
}
```

Passing the event's attributes along tells wrangler which request to approve. Roles arrive from the receiving pico's point of view: `Rx_role` is this pico's, and `Tx_role` is the other pico's.

Don't approve every request. A rule without a `where` accepts a relationship with any pico that has your well-known channel. Accept only what you expect: the right roles, a request from your parent, a request that carries a shared secret. To refuse, raise `wrangler:inbound_rejection` with the same attributes. The [Collection](/cookbook/collection/) demo does both, and remembers whom it turned away.

## Wrangler's auto-accept configuration

Without writing a rule, give the participant a pattern to accept:

```krl
raise wrangler event "autoAcceptConfigUpdate" attributes {
  "config": {"configName": "lists", "entries": {"Tx_role": ["^participant list$"]}}
}
```

Each entry maps an attribute of the request, as the participant sees it, to a list of regular expressions. A request that matches any of them is approved. Send the same event with `"delete": true` and the `configName` to remove it. `autoAcceptConfig()`, shared by `io.picolabs.subscription`, shows what is set. You can also send this event from the pico's **Testing** tab.

## Accept later, by installing a ruleset

If a request arrived before there was anything to approve it, install a ruleset that approves it and then removes itself:

```krl
ruleset acceptance {
  meta {
    use module io.picolabs.subscription alias subs
  }
  rule initialize {
    select when wrangler ruleset_installed where event:attr("rids") >< meta:rid
    pre {
      s = subs:inbound("Tx_role", "participant list")
        .filter(function(i) { i{"Rx_role"} == "participant" })
        .head()
    }
    if s then noop()
    fired {
      raise wrangler event "pending_subscription_approval" attributes s
    }
    finally {
      raise wrangler event "uninstall_ruleset_request" attributes {"rid": meta:rid}
    }
  }
}
```

It looks for a pending request from a participant list, approves it, and uninstalls itself either way. This is handy when a parent asked many children to join before they could accept: install it on each child.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook pages "Automatic Replies to Subscription Requests" and "Accepting a subscription offer by installing a ruleset".*


---

# Tip: one pico per resource

# One pico per resource

Some things should be used by only one party at a time: a motor, a GPIO pin, a printer, an account with an outside service. Give each one its own pico. Everything else asks that pico, by event, to use the resource. Because a pico handles one event at a time, its rulesets are the only code that touches the resource, and requests can't collide.

A Pico Labs rover project did this with its wheels. Each of four wheel picos kept the index of the one motor it drove, and only its rules called the motor driver:

```krl
rule set_motor_index {
  select when rover motor_index_assigned
  always {
    ent:motor_index := event:attr("motor_index")
  }
}
```

A controller pico had a channel to each wheel. To move, it sent each wheel the direction that wheel should turn:

```krl
to_wheels = defaction(type, fr, fl, br, bl) {
  every {
    event:send({"eci": ent:wheels{"FR"}, "domain": "rover", "type": type, "attrs": fr})
    event:send({"eci": ent:wheels{"FL"}, "domain": "rover", "type": type, "attrs": fl})
    event:send({"eci": ent:wheels{"BR"}, "domain": "rover", "type": type, "attrs": br})
    event:send({"eci": ent:wheels{"BL"}, "domain": "rover", "type": type, "attrs": bl})
  }
}
forward = defaction() {
  to_wheels("run", {"direction": "fwd"}, {"direction": "back"}, {"direction": "back"}, {"direction": "fwd"})
}
```

The controller could have driven the motors itself. But then every new pico that needed the wheels would need the motor code too, and two of them could drive the same motor at once. With a pico per wheel, any number of controllers can share the wheels safely.

Keep the channels to the resource picos in relationships (or, for children, in their family channels), not in ECIs written into the code. The original rover hard-coded them, and noted that relationships would be much better.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook page "Singleton Pattern".*


---

# Tip: hosting and checking rulesets

# Hosting and checking rulesets

## Install from a URL

The engine installs a ruleset from a URL and remembers it. A few kinds work well:

- **Your own files**, while you work: `file:///path/to/my.ruleset.krl`. The engine must be on the same machine.
- **GitHub**: use the *raw* URL, `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch>/<path>.krl`, not the page that displays the file.
- **The engine's own**: `http://<engine>/krl/<rid>.krl` for the rulesets that ship with it, and `/krl/demos/...` for the demos.

## Flush after you change it

The engine compiles a ruleset once and keeps it. After you change the source, click **Flush** next to the ruleset on the pico's **Rulesets** tab, and the engine fetches the URL again. Every pico with that ruleset gets the new version.

Flushing doesn't raise `wrangler:ruleset_installed` again, so rules that run on install don't run. If you change what such a rule sets up, such as a channel's policy, run that rule again yourself. The [Bootstrap and channels](/cookbook/bootstrap/) demo shows how.

## Check before you commit

`krl-check` parses and compiles KRL, and lints doc comments and views. It ships with `krl-compiler`:

```sh
npm install -g krl-compiler
krl-check my.ruleset.krl
```

It exits with status 1 on an error and prints warnings to stderr. With no file, it reads standard input. That makes a Git pre-commit hook that checks exactly what you're about to commit. Save this as `.git/hooks/pre-commit` and make it executable:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
status=0
for f in $(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM -- '*.krl'); do
  if ! git show ":$f" | krl-check >/dev/null; then
    echo "krl-check failed: $f"
    status=1
  fi
done
exit $status
```

`git show ":$f"` is the staged version of the file, so a fix you haven't staged yet doesn't hide an error.

*From the Pico Labs KRL Cookbook pages "Hosting Code on GitHub" and "Setting Up a Git Pre-Commit Hook to Parse KRL".*


---

# Bundled rulesets

# Bundled rulesets (generated docs)

These are API references: every documented event and function of each ruleset. For guides to what they're for and how they fit together, see [Wrangler](/wrangler/).

Markdown here is copied from `tools/krl-schema/samples/` when you run **`npm run generate:llms`** at the repo root. Sources are the annotated KRL under `packages/pico-engine/krl/`. To regenerate samples from KRL: **`npm run check:krl-schema-samples`** (CI) or `node tools/krl-schema/cli.js -f markdown path/to/ruleset.krl`.

## OS layer (every pico)

Installed on the root pico and on each new child automatically.

| Ruleset | Doc |
|---------|-----|
| **io.picolabs.wrangler** | [wrangler](io.picolabs.wrangler.md) — **pico OS**; the supported API for mesh lifecycle (not raw `ctx:*`). If an operation is missing here, treat it as out-of-bounds or [file an engine issue](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/issues). |
| **io.picolabs.pds** | [pds](io.picolabs.pds.md) — profile and shared namespaced data |
| **io.picolabs.subscription** | [subscription](io.picolabs.subscription.md) — relationships to other picos |
| **io.picolabs.pico-engine-ui** | [pico-engine-ui](io.picolabs.pico-engine-ui.md) — developer UI channel |

## Optional (install when needed)

Shipped under `/krl/` on your engine; install from the Rulesets tab or `wrangler:install_ruleset_request` with the ruleset URL.

| Ruleset | Doc | Notes |
|---------|-----|--------|
| **io.picolabs.oauth** | [oauth](io.picolabs.oauth.md) | **Root pico only** — optional mesh-wide OAuth on `/sky/*` |
| **io.picolabs.portable_subtree** | [portable_subtree](io.picolabs.portable_subtree.md) | Portable export/import of subtrees (identity-aware move) |
| **io.picolabs.xmlui** | [Pico views](../pico-views.md) | Optional. A `@view` function is a page at `/ui/{eci}/{rid}/`; a `@component` function is a reusable part. Ships the `PicoTheme`, `PicoSettings`, `PicoThemeField`, and `PicoAccessTokenField` components |

Application rulesets (Manifold, your apps) are not bundled; install their KRL URLs like any other ruleset.

# KRL manual

# KRL Manual

KRL (the Kinetic Rule Language) is the language picos are programmed in. A KRL **ruleset** is a set of rules that react to events and functions that answer queries; installing a ruleset in a pico gives that pico new behavior.

New to KRL? Start with the [Overview](/krl/overview/), then read [Rulesets](/krl/rulesets/) and [Event Expressions](/krl/event-expressions/).

## Contents

- [Overview](/krl/overview/)
- [Rulesets](/krl/rulesets/)
- [Event Expressions](/krl/event-expressions/)
- [KRL Expression Language](/krl/krl-expression-language/)
- [Libraries](/krl/libraries/)
- [Discovery](/krl/discovery)
- [Persistent Variables](/krl/persistent-variables/)
- [Grammar](/krl/grammar)
- [User Defined Modules](/krl/user-defined-modules)

> **Note:** Most of this manual was ported from the [Pico Labs wiki](https://picolabs.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/docs/pages/1189890/KRL+Manual), and some pages describe the classic (pre-Node) engine. Each ported page links back to its wiki original and shows when it was last edited there. Corrections are welcome as pull requests against `docs/krl/` in [Picolab/pico-engine](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine).


---

# Contributing

# Contributing


To run the pico-engine in development mode do the following:

```sh
$ git clone https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine.git
$ cd pico-engine
$ npm run setup
$ npm start
```

That will start the server and run the test. `npm start` is simply an alias for `cd packages/pico-engine && npm start`

**NOTE about dependencies:** generally don't use `npm i`, rather use `npm run setup` from the root. [lerna](https://github.com/lerna/lerna) will link up the packages so when you make changes in one package, it will be used in others.

## Improving documentation

This documentation site is found in the [docs](https://github.com/Picolab/pico-engine/tree/master/docs) folder at the repository root. The pages are simple markdown files. It uses [docsify](https://docsify.js.org/) to serve it.

To preview changes run the docsify local server using `npm run docs`. Then open your browser to the "Listening at" url.

## Making changes

Use a branch (or fork) to do your work. When you are ready, create a pull request. That way we can review it before merging it into master. (See the git cheatsheet below)

### git cheatsheet

```sh
# list your checked out branches
git branch

# list all branches including remote ones you don't have checked out
git branch -a

# checkout a remote branch
git checkout -t origin/<branch>

# switch branches
git checkout <branch>
git checkout master

# create a new branch off master
git checkout -b <branch> master

# push your local branch to github
git push -u origin <branch>

# to update your branch with the latest in master
git checkout master
git pull
git checkout <branch>
git merge master


# Use github to merge your branch into master using a pull request.
# On github use the "new pull request" button to make a PR for merging.
# Once the PR is merged you can delete the branch using the button on github.


# Even though the branch is deleted on github, it won't delete it off your local machine.
# to delete a local branch
git branch -d <branch>
```
